# Error Handling, Retries, and Reliable Workflows

## Overview
Beginners build automations that work on the happy path; professionals build automations that keep working when things go wrong, and this reliability mindset is what separates a hobby project from production. Automations fail for many reasons: an API is temporarily down, returns an error, or rate-limits you; incoming data is missing a field or malformed; a service changes; or a downstream app rejects the request. If you ignore these, your automation silently breaks and nobody notices until damage is done. The solutions are learnable patterns. Error handlers (Make.com has dedicated error-handler routes, n8n has error workflows, Zapier has built-in retries and error emails) let you catch a failure and decide what to do instead of just crashing. Retries automatically re-attempt a failed step, ideally with exponential backoff (wait longer between each try) so a brief outage self-heals without hammering the API. Fallback paths and default values keep the workflow moving when optional data is missing - if there is no phone number, proceed without it rather than failing. Alerting is crucial: when something truly fails, the automation should notify you (a Slack alert, an email) so you can react quickly. Finally, idempotency - designing steps so that running them twice does not cause double charges or duplicate records - protects you when retries happen. Building in error handling from the start, rather than bolting it on after an incident, is exactly the discipline employers expect from a dependable automation engineer.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: Why automations fail (API errors, bad data, downtime); Error handlers and try/catch-style routes; Retries and exponential backoff; Fallback paths and default values; Alerting on failures and idempotency. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
**Practical Task:** Take an existing workflow and add error handling: configure a retry on a flaky step, add a fallback for a missing field, and send yourself an alert message if the workflow ultimately fails.
**Mini Project:** Build a robust API-sync workflow with a dedicated error-handling route that retries transient failures, logs permanent failures to a sheet, sends an alert, and is idempotent so re-runs never create duplicates.
**Assignment:** List five ways an automation can fail and, for each, describe the specific handling strategy (retry, fallback, alert, skip, or idempotency) you would apply and why.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.
